How does Lyra (Lyra 1 not 2) compare to Balloon, Argon2, and Lyra2?
I'm looking for something simple, preferably generic sponge/hash based. I hoped BKDF will be that.

comments.author: solardiz
comments.body:
@LightBit I didn't recall (it's been a decade), but I've just skimmed the Lyra paper again. I think Lyra is much more practical compared to Balloon (it uses larger blocks aka longer rows), and is on par with scrypt. It claims (and perhaps actually achieves) some TMTO resistance (unlike scrypt, which is deliberately TMTO-friendly). I expect its actual TMTO resistance may vary by the sponge's internal state size (those mentioned for suggested sponges are somewhat small, in hundreds of bits vs. yescrypt's 12 KiB). This internal state is also what discourages sub-block (aka column) pipelining attacks, where scrypt uses sub-block shuffling instead (so Lyra managed to simplify this out). However, Argon2 designers' "Tradeoff Cryptanalysis of Memory-Hard Functions" claims even Lyra2 is vulnerable: "the time-memory product for Lyra2 can be decreased by the factor of 8." I don't recall the detail, such as whether the Lyra2 designers provided a response and what it was.

Incidentally, I admit I didn't get those pipelining attacks before that paper (it was eye-opening for me, even though @cperciva clearly had thought of them during scrypt design), and I adjusted the final yescrypt design in response. This is where yescrypt block function's rapidly updated internal state appeared. But to my knowledge, those attacks were not of practical help against actual uses of earlier yescrypt drafts for PoW and thus mining on GPUs. Maybe they would be on ASICs.

Lyra's reported defensive speeds when instantiated with a BLAKE2-based sponge are on par with scrypt. It uses data-dependent addressing (which makes me wonder why they suggest higher than minimum T - perhaps again a chase for academic levels of TMTO resistance beyond practical reason, same as we see in recommended parameters for Balloon and Argon2). Lyra2 is a safer bet, given it's a newer yet already mature revision, and is PHC's special recognition. It's also only moderately more complex. It further improves TMTO resistance while achieving similar speeds, and integrates BlaMka (for multiplication latency hardening, which is also implemented in Argon2 and yescrypt).

So if you really want a single-primitive scheme and don't mind the sub-block pipelining risk (which apparently no one exploited in practice so far), Lyra2 isn't bad, and even the original Lyra looks adequate too. However, what single primitive would that be? With the recommended ones based on pieces from BLAKE2, you'd have the same standards compliance issues as with Argon2.

In (ye)scrypt, at least you have entropy bypass via proven and standards-compliant HMAC and SHA-256, so you can prove that basic cryptographic properties are inherited from those primitives (even if the heavy processing completely fails, like returns all zeroes). For scrypt, this is the case for the password input to hash output. For yescrypt, it's also for the salt input.

I see you've already implemented scrypt before, so you actually know it's not all that complex. Why not just continue using it if you don't want anything more complex and are fine with data-dependent indexing? https://github.com/LightBit/libkripto/blob/master/lib/scrypt.c

comments.author: LightBit
comments.body:
@solardiz Thanks. Will check this paper and Lyra2 revisions.
Its not really hard to implement with reference implementation available, but I prefer simpler designs that are easy to understand (idealy so simple you can implement it from head).

comments.author: samuel-lucas6
comments.body:
Sorry for the delayed response again.

> For Argon2 as we currently have it in JtR, this point is in the hundreds of megabytes, which is rather high.
> ... although some other attacker would choose a bcrypt-friendlier GPU instead (perhaps recent NVIDIA).

Thank you @solardiz, I see. How equivalent is increasing the iterations with lower memory?

> I couldn't quickly find where they say "the Argon2 round function can be made more sequential".

A summary is on page 8, and the more detailed version is Section 7. They modify the round function by adding some data-dependencies using XOR. According to the authors, it roughly preserves defender performance whilst slowing down the attacker.

> To me, trapdoor memory-hard functions sound like they're for some different use cases, and I wonder what those would be.

From that conversation, my understanding was the user keeps a secret key, whereas the server stores a public key (kind of like passkeys). The user can compute the output using little memory, whereas the server has to use lots of memory. That way, if the server is compromised, an attacker has to use lots of memory as well. Although this seems kind of backwards in that servers may be more limited than clients since they have to handle multiple clients.

My thinking for why it's worse than a pepper/encrypting hashes is that those approaches prevent password cracking completely unless the secret is known. And even if the secret is known, you still have the memory-hard function to slow down cracking. With trapdoor MHFs, it sounds like a compromise of the secret ruins the defence in terms of memory. They're also more complicated to understand and implement, so it doesn't sound like they'll take off. PAKEs don't seem to have been that successful, and now we have passkeys assuming the UX gets sorted.

> As to pepper, to me it's clear (and was at the time of PHC) that we need hash encryption instead of pepper (which is why yescrypt only has hash encryption). It's as good as pepper, but it also allows for key change (if potentially compromised). Doing it without dependency on an extra primitive is a bit tricky. yescrypt has a custom Feistel cipher based on SHA-256. It's not very complex, but I understand that when you optimize for simplicity, you implement a pepper instead.

I agree for password hashing. However, I think a pepper makes sense for key derivation in that it's one-way like the rest of key derivation.

The nice thing about a design like Finnick is because it's based on an encryption algorithm, you can use the underlying function for that purpose.

> Looks like you misunderstood me. I didn't comment on Argon2's explicit/configurable parallelism at all. I commented on the lower-level parallelism hard-coded in its block function

Ah, sorry. I think I see what you mean. You've made a lot of nice presentations I need to take a look at.

> Sure AES can be fast on GPUs, but AES-NI makes it faster than other primitives on CPUs, so the GPU advantage is reduced. As to this specific paper, we actually looked into it and made code changes in JtR accordingly:

That makes sense. I'm surprised there hasn't been more use of AES, although I suppose hardware support has increased since the PHC. Do you think lack of support is really a problem now? I would think it's mainly an issue for embedded devices, which aren't going to be using a memory-hard function anyway.

> I'm looking for something simple, preferably generic sponge/hash based. I hoped BKDF will be that.

@LightBit so did I. The issue is standard hash functions don't seem ideal for this purpose. You want something with a larger output and a function that's suboptimal for hardware (aka not SHA-3, which is obviously the main sponge-based family and going to become more popular with PQC). And if the password hashing algorithm is significantly slower than alternatives, it shouldn't be used from a security standpoint because you're weakening yourself.

I like simplicity a lot too, but it may be the best password hashing algorithms need to be a bit more complex, which definitely isn't the case with some other types of algorithm. Having said that, perhaps cache-hard algorithms don't need to be as complicated. There needs to be more documentation on them.

> perhaps again a chase for academic levels of TMTO resistance beyond practical reason, same as we see in recommended parameters for Balloon and Argon2

Which parameters are you talking about? Do you mean like increasing the delta in Balloon, high memory/iterations, or something else? The Argon2 RFC has very high memory recommendations that don't sound practical.

comments.author: solardiz
comments.body:
> How equivalent is increasing the iterations with lower memory?

I'm not sure I get this question. Do you mean when memory usage is so low anyway that we haven't yet reached the point where increases of it slow down GPUs more than CPUs? If so, there's in fact a range of parameters where increasing iterations is only slightly less effective against GPUs than increasing memory, as either parameter has a close to linear effect. However, increasing memory _is_ slightly more effective - and more than slightly against ASICs - even at these low parameters.

Where I mentioned that a Monero ASIC at 2 MiB was ~100x more power-efficient than CPUs and GPUs, you need to consider that the factor of ~100x is still way lower than it'd have been for PBKDF2 (~1k vs. GPUs and ~10k vs. CPUs, as we see from Bitcoin mining).

> > I couldn't quickly find where they say "the Argon2 round function can be made more sequential".
> 
> A summary is on page 8, and the more detailed version is Section 7. They modify the round function by adding some data-dependencies using XOR. According to the authors, it roughly preserves defender performance whilst slowing down the attacker.

Oh, sure. I wish they clearly marked the changes in the referenced GitHub repo, such as made them a separate commit.

But anyway, yes, this was a known property of Argon2, and yes it could be made more sequential without decrease in throughput on a server, see e.g. last paragraph in my comment below comparing memory bandwidth usage with yescrypt, which has 6x more sequential multiplication latency hardening:

https://github.com/P-H-C/phc-winner-argon2/issues/231

Further, in there I show that even higher defensive speeds are possible despite of the more sequential computation if the block size is increased a bit (it's fixed at 1 KiB in Argon2, but is configurable in (ye)scrypt, so for yescrypt I currently recommend 4 KiB).

Also see the `COMPARISON` in my upstream yescrypt tree and on its homepage. Which, by the way, I had asked others on the PHC list to comment when the list was still operational (even though PHC was over), but no one did, so I assume I got everything right.

Unfortunately, many in PHC were too focused on single thread latency under low load, whereas what limits the parameter values on servers is throughput under load spike or simulated DoS-like conditions. When I was consulting on yescrypt deployments, the task was always to achieve this-many requests per second per server at full (aka abnormally high) load. Latency also mattered, but again under those same max concurrent load conditions (latency under low load is then obviously acceptable and more stable anyway).

On trapdoors:

> From that conversation, my understanding was the user keeps a secret key, whereas the server stores a public key (kind of like passkeys). The user can compute the output using little memory, whereas the server has to use lots of memory.

Oh, then my _guess_ is it may be intended as a way to authenticate quickly while the secret key is available, but also be able to authenticate (slower) even if the secret key is lost. This makes some sense then. However, in a resource exhaustion DoS attack the slow, server-heavy path would be triggered all the time. So this accepts that this slow/recovery path may have worse availability (the server may have to disallow it first while under attack).

> My thinking for why it's worse than a pepper/encrypting hashes is that those approaches prevent password cracking completely unless the secret is known.

Yes, but maybe they have different goals - see above. Also, maybe they can co-exist with hash encryption on server.

> I think a pepper makes sense for key derivation in that it's one-way like the rest of key derivation.

With key derivation, where would you store the pepper such that it'd not always leak when the salt does? Well, maybe smartcard/TPM could have it, but salts be part of encrypted files.

As to it being one-way, what does this buy us? I think almost nothing. If we compare against encryption of the KDF output, which can be reversed, it's just a tiny fraction of the total running time of the KDF. Sure a password cracker could reverse it at startup, but with a heavy enough KDF the overall effect of that reversal would be negligible. So I think it's preferable not to special-case the KDF use case, and only have hash/KDF encryption rather than pepper.

> I'm surprised there hasn't been more use of AES, although I suppose hardware support has increased since the PHC. Do you think lack of support is really a problem now?

It's less of a problem than it was at the time of PHC. However, I think the biggest issue is that when using AES, we have to supply a software AES implementation in the tree anyway, even if it would be very rarely used. Also separate code for x86 and ARM, or else ARM would fallback to software and not only be slower but also have extra side-channel leaks. So the source tree is complicated significantly. Unless it's a higher-level implementation that uses a library that has AES anyway. Further, if you use not the full AES, but pieces from it (like individual rounds), then you generally can't rely on a library providing those (have to carry your own).

> perhaps cache-hard algorithms don't need to be as complicated.

Unfortunately, cache-hard-only algorithms only defend against GPUs, somewhat against FPGAs (if targeting L2+ cache on CPUs, not L1 like bcrypt did), and do quite little against ASICs. Also, no attempt to make them data-independent so far.

The cache-hardness in yescrypt adds little complexity on top of what yescrypt needed anyway. Maybe even none. The internal state is also needed against sub-block pipelining anyway.

> > perhaps again a chase for academic levels of TMTO resistance beyond practical reason, same as we see in recommended parameters for Balloon and Argon2
> 
> Which parameters are you talking about?

The "time complexity" or t_cost or t or T or iterations, whatever it's called in a given algorithm. The academic preference was to set it high enough that TMTO resistance is obviously prohibitively high. However, this fails to consider that setting it lower enables much higher total defensive memory usage in same total running time, so even moderately effective TMTO would still result in higher memory usage since the starting point would have been so much higher. Like "one half of 30 MB" (lowest t_cost, 30 MB total, lowered by a factor of 2 by TMTO in an attack) vs. "all of 10 MB" (t_cost=3 defeating that TMTO "fully", but limiting defender's usage to 10 MB). For practical purposes, from a defender's perspective, 15 MB post-TMTO is better than 10 MB without TMTO.

And yes, in Balloon also delta, but if instantiated with a slow primitive like SHA-512 this doesn't hurt - doesn't slow it down much _more_ on top of the slow primitive. So it's actually reasonable to have high delta on top of that. It wouldn't be so reasonable with a properly fast large-output primitive.

> The Argon2 RFC has very high memory recommendations that don't sound practical.

The Argon2 RFC's section "[4. ](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106.html#section-4)[Parameter Choice](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9106.html#name-parameter-choice)" looks detached from reality. Not only are those target runtimes much higher than what's typically required for authentication, but they also suggest usage of 2+ lanes even for cryptocurrency mining and authentication. Somehow I see the RFC lists me among those "who helped in preparing and reviewing this document", which I appreciate, but I don't recall reviewing these parameters. On the bright side, they do appear to favor t=1. :-)

comments.author: solardiz
comments.body:
> in Balloon also delta, but if instantiated with a slow primitive like SHA-512 this doesn't hurt - doesn't slow it down much _more_ on top of the slow primitive. So it's actually reasonable to have high delta on top of that.

Sorry, I misrecalled how Balloon works. Higher delta increases the number of hash computations (the way the algorithm is given in the paper) or at least the amount of data to hash (the way you have it in the BKDF spec), not only the number of memory reads (as I had wrongly recalled), so it makes e.g. SHA-512 a lot slower at producing output. So the same concerns apply as to higher t_cost. This probably _does_ result in a lot lower s_cost, and any changes in TMTO resistance should be considered with that in mind, not on their own.

comments.author: solardiz
comments.body: @samuel-lucas6 I found the discussion you had in https://crypto.stackexchange.com/questions/114049/whats-the-use-of-the-delta-parameter-in-balloons-hash and also took a fresh look at the Balloon paper. In that StackExchange discussion, the comment by n-l-i is helpful, but it somehow assumes t_cost does not contribute to TMTO resistance at all, whereas I think it also does. The attacks on Argon2i (specific to data-independent indexing) in the Balloon paper give different TMTO factors depending on t_cost, namely 1/4 for lowest t_cost (single-pass) vs. 1/e for high t_cost (a very impressive result). I see how the 1/4 vs. 1/e difference may be deemed insignificant compared to the greater effect delta has. So maybe in Balloon / BKDF delta=3 is actually optimal. You also don't want lower delta because you'd deviate from Balloon, which would partially defeat the purpose of this project.

comments.author: solardiz
comments.body: I forgot that Argon2i has been updated to address those attacks. They were for version 1.2.1, whereas in version 1.3 that is in use now "The blocks are XORed with, not overwritten in the second pass and later". I see that Balloon also processes the block being written to as input, which should have similar effect. With this, I expect that increases in t_cost should have significant effect on TMTO resistance of both Argon2i and Balloon/BKDF. However, this is not a reason to use delta lower than 3 and compensate for that with higher t_cost. Either high delta or high t_cost result in lower s_cost anyway. So delta=3, t_cost=1, and s_cost as high as affordable looks reasonable for Balloon.

comments.author: solardiz
comments.body:
> Getting the right block size was one thing I wasn't sure about with Finnick.

Yes, it's tricky. You need to optimize defensive (vs. offensive) speeds for direct computation, but also consider that the way you process sub-blocks in a block may be vulnerable to pipelining. So in yescrypt I wouldn't recommend blocks larger than pwxform's internal state (currently 12 KiB). Luckily, defensive speeds are good at 4 KiB, so we don't reach that level.

Also consider that by a larger block, you may be taking more of your defensive cache space away from possible more cache-hardness. OTOH, without deliberate cache-hardness in the algorithm anyway, using a larger block size may provide a tiny bit of poor man's cache-hardness-alike (CPU will have the previous block in cache, but GPU at high concurrency might have to re-fetch it piece-by-piece, or otherwise have its concurrency more limited) - but this is a risky bet.

> Got it, so a combined approach is probably best. Do you know why [Argon2ds](https://www.password-hashing.net/argon2-specs.pdf) never took off?

I don't know exactly why, but I suspect it's because:
1. PHC chose Argon2 as the winner largely for what the judges saw as simplicity (although to me it doesn't actually look simpler than scrypt). Any extras would go against that.
2. 2id and 2ds were late optional mode additions. Since 2id did take off, this means that this alone isn't enough of a reason why 2ds did not.
3. The reference PHC tree at https://github.com/P-H-C/phc-winner-argon2 added 2id, but not 2ds. So it was this tree maintainers' decision to support/promote 2id and not 2ds. They understandably didn't want too many variants.
4. That decision may have been based on already existing demand/criticism. As I recall, 2id was in fact requested by some on the PHC list.
5. No 2ids mode was defined. If someone wanted defense against cache timing, they had to choose 2i or 2id. So 2id it was.
6. Out of most-active participants on the PHC list, the properties of 2ds in a candidate algorithm (that is, sequential memory-hard and also [what later became known as] cache-hard) were requested by Bill Cox @waywardgeek and me. But both of us had our own candidates, and yescrypt got special recognition. So Argon2ds would be kind of redundant with yescrypt.
7. Password crackers were late to add Argon2 support/attacks. Our integration of Argon2 OpenCL code into JtR is late 2023. We don't yet have yescrypt 1.0 in OpenCL, at all. So we're just now starting to truly show what these differences mean in practice.

BTW, 2ds adds not only cache-hardness, but also latency hardening - both on par with yescrypt 0.5, which is not a coincidence. But differently from yescrypt, IIRC it uses the approach that TwoCats also chose - the latency-hardened chain is scalar. So while the SIMD units compute the 1 KiB block in parallel, scalar units have to go through the 96 rounds sequentially. This means that there's a lot less computation total (sequential times parallel) in that chain (compared to yescrypt's way of doing cache-hardness and latency hardening as part of its main block processing on SIMD units). But most of the desired effect should be achieved anyway.

> Also, is there any good reading material besides your [yescrypt specification](https://www.password-hashing.net/submissions/specs/yescrypt-v2.pdf) for understanding how to implement cache-hardness?

Unfortunately, no. The best reading material may be PHC list postings by Bill Cox and me. ;-)

The way I approached it, I always kept two kinds of attack in mind - with S-boxes in local vs. global memory. In bcrypt, the lookups are so tiny and frequent that only local memory attacks are practical. (You can do global memory indeed, but it's just slower. You could maybe do both at once for higher cumulative throughput, which we briefly attempted, but no luck so far.)

As you start increasing the S-boxes to target L2+ rather than L1 cache, and have to make lookups less frequent, you on one hand make local memory attacks even slower, but on the other hand make global memory attacks more practical. In other words, target too high a cache level and size, and you're no longer local memory hard, so this stops being a separate defense.

The width of lookups also matters, but there's no drawback from wider lookups for the defender as long as this width increase does not make them less frequent nor less numerous nor more parallel. This is why bcrypt 32-bit vs. yescrypt 128-bit does not make yescrypt weaker in typical builds.

During PHC, I felt that being obviously/provably (by specific metrics) no worse (or at least not much worse) than bcrypt is the important goal. So all of yescrypt, TwoCats, and Argon2ds target L1 cache by default. Later yescrypt 0.5 mining results on specific GPUs (circa 2018) show that this was still pretty effective, but there was room for improvement, at least short-term to satisfy the needs of some altcoins. So while yescrypt 1.0 uses 12 KiB, yespower 1.0 went to 96 KiB at twice fewer pwxform rounds (so twice less frequent lookups against mostly L2 cache, increasing vulnerability to global memory attacks but not enough to make them most practical). I conservatively kept it at 128-bit lookup width (to be able to reason based on existing yescrypt 0.5 mining speeds), although going for 512-bit is also reasonable when targeting L2+ cache (but would be harder to predict the full effect of). All of these choices were based on benchmarks on hardware most relevant at the time.

The way yescrypt/yespower pwxform is defined, all of these things are tunable (currently compile-time). You may want to see these slides: https://www.openwall.com/presentations/BSidesLjubljana2017-Yescrypt-Large-scale-Password-Hashing/slide-044.html

With today's L1d commonly increased from 32 to 48 KiB, I'd probably choose at least 24 KiB for yescrypt, but for now I feel this is not enough of a reason to re-tune and introduce a variation.

> It would be nice to have as few parameters as possible, like PBKDF2/bcrypt, but I guess that's not possible without leaving some extra security on the table.

Right, but it's reasonable to have a wrapper that would map one parameter onto the rest, with the full derived parameter set recorded along with the hashes. This is done in libxcrypt for yescrypt:

https://github.com/besser82/libxcrypt/blob/e34e0634a7192383dbb4445b6d7568e36baef675/lib/crypt-yescrypt.c#L136

issues.title: Nice-to-have features
issues.author: jedisct1
issues.body:
Some nice-to-have features. That may be out of scope for that document, but that would solve some real-world problems that all the widely used password hashing algorithms have.

1) Server relief. Allow the client to perform a part of the computation. In BKDF, `hash` is just the addition of the outputs of independent `BalloonCore` instantiations, so that can easily be implemented. Provided that `pepper` is empty, or can be computed as a shared secret.

2) Encryption. Section 9 refers to it, but maybe it would be an opportunity to define a standard way to do it. Introducing a dependency on AEADs is not required. Encryption can be made by leveraging the PRF.

3) The ability to upgrade parameters without having access to the passwords, similar to libhydrogen's [pwhash_upgrade](https://github.com/jedisct1/libhydrogen/wiki/Password-hashing#updating-the-parameters) function. That would be a killer feature. In BKDF, the only way to achieve that would be to define a way to encode the composition of multiple BKDF calls. Probably out of scope for the document. But damn, that's something that would be really amazing to have in new password hashing functions.

comments.author: samuel-lucas6
comments.body: Thanks for these suggestions. Definitely worth thinking about. I never considered 1 with the same computation rather than calling the entire algorithm twice. For 2, the dilemma would probably be the conflict with the `pepper` parameter and maybe the output length. 3 would be nice but isn't something I've read into.
